title: The Old Roof
logline: A household strips every leaf off its roof and weaves on new ones, and by their own account it is still the same roof, though nothing that was on it before is on it now.
human_question: When something continues, what exactly is it that continues?

situation.what_happens: A household renews a roof that is made of something perishable and has to be remade every few years. The old material is stripped off entirely, and for a stretch of hours or days there is no roof at all, only the frame. New material is prepared and woven on, by older hands who have done it many times and younger ones who are picking it up as they go. When it is finished the family calls it the same roof they have always had, and they are not being sentimental: it is the thing they live under, in the same place, doing the same job, with nothing old left in it. Meanwhile the people who depend on the roof, and the neighbours who come to help, carry on underneath a house that has been continuous for years without any of its parts being so.
situation.who_is_involved: The household who live under it; the older members or neighbours who know how the weaving is done and are effectively teaching it while working; the younger ones learning by hand, who will hold the skill after the people who taught them are gone; and whoever else in the settlement depends on the same renewal happening to their own house.
situation.what_is_at_stake: Shelter, and whether the work continues to be done this way at all. Every renewal is also a decision: to keep spending days on a roof that must be redone, or to change to something that does not need renewing, which would end both the work and the passing-on of the skill. There is also what happens if the weather turns during the gap when there is no roof.
situation.how_it_unfolds: A renewal like this begins with a roof that is visibly failing, opens into a period when the house is not weatherproof at all, and closes with a finished roof or a household deciding this was the last time. What the family concludes about whether to keep doing it, and whether the younger hands actually take the skill on, is decided by them.

concept_merge.why_together: C081 supplies the two methods held together: the method of identity, which sees unbroken continuity, and the method of diversity, which sees each stage as new and distinct — each one correcting an error the other would produce if taken alone. C080 supplies what the continuity is made of, and its images are exactly this ordinary: milk and curd, a lamp lit from another lamp, a man crossing a stream on a rope tied to a tree on the near bank who lands by his own weight with nothing of that bank coming with him, and clearest of all, a skill learned as a child that lives on in the adult's hands and in no one else's. A roof remade leaf by leaf, by hands that were taught by the hands before them, holds both at once: a thing continuous with nothing carried across, and a skill continuous in exactly the same way.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: Put together, they make the difficult middle position liveable rather than paradoxical: not the same, not something else, and no traveller inside it. What becomes visible is that the continuity people actually rely on — of a house, of a craft, of a person — has never depended on anything persisting unchanged, so the texts' refusal of a thing that moves across is not a loss of continuity but a description of the only kind there ever was.

concept_links.why: The Pradeepika's methods of identity and diversity are meant to be held together: seen alone, continuity suggests something unchanging running through, and difference suggests no relation at all. A roof that is wholly renewed and still theirs sits exactly between the two errors each method is said to prevent.

The source says nothing comes over from what went before and yet nothing appears without a cause: if the two were simply the same, curd could not come from milk, and if simply different, curd would have nothing to do with milk. Its plainest image is a skill learned in childhood living on in the adult's hands and going to no one else, which a renewal taught hand to hand shows directly.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: A roof can be the same roof for years although every part of it has been replaced. The texts describe a life in a similar way: not exactly the same as before, not something else, and with nothing carried across.
what_must_be_real: Whether the household still wants to do this at all, and their own reasons either way. The renewal must be one they were going to do, and the film may not encourage them to keep a practice they would rather give up.
position_hint: middle: it takes the previous film's support-at-one-moment and carries it across time, and it prepares the group's later claim that what is held up by conditions ends when they stop.
risks: Treating the household as picturesque, or implying that traditional work is better for them than the alternative they may prefer.
Letting the roof be read as a soul passing on; the texts reject exactly that view, and the roof is only an everyday picture of continuity without a traveller.
Loading the family's ordinary words about their house with a doctrinal meaning they did not intend.
drop_if: No household renews by hand within the filming window.
The work can only be filmed by asking for it to be done earlier or differently than planned.

connections.note: Both follow a craft that renews itself hand by hand, one entering a length anywhere, the other replacing every part and staying the same thing.
A structure that holds by leaning at one moment is followed by a structure that holds across years by being wholly replaced.

selection.reason: Used by EPD-0084; enlarged by the crossing idea so that C080 is now carried as a primary link rather than only in support.

unknowns: No participant or event has been found or confirmed. Everything here is a research direction.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. No location, scene or shot decisions are made at the idea stage.
